newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China takes major step on to world oil stage.
newsitem.headline: China takes major step on to world oil stage.

text.p: China's deals with Iraq and Kazakhstan have moved it a big step forward in the international oil markets and point to a more aggressive search for foreign crude supplies, analysts said on Thursday.
Analysts expressed some doubts on Wednesday's pact with Kazakhstan for a 3,000 km (2,000 mile) pipeline into Xinjiang, saying the northwestern Chinese province had an oil surplus.

"Xinjiang already has more than enough oil which China is trying to transport to the east," said U.S.-based Asia-Pacific energy analyst Kang Wu. "The pipeline project is a little remote at the moment. It could take a long time to realise."
But the China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) also signed a $1.2 billion deal on Wednesday with Baghdad to develop the one-billion-barrel Ahdab oil field in the south of Iraq.

"This is a very big step for China," said Wu, noting the investment was one of CNPC's biggest and that buying equity stakes to guarantee supplies was likely to be a major plank in China's new strategy.
"The limited reserves in China make it inevitable to import, and equity investment means China can secure the resources in other countries," Wu said.
In 1996, China's proven oil reserves stood at 24 billion barrels, or just 2.4 percent of the world reserves, Wu said.
Competition was tough for the Iraq deal as over 50 foreign firms had been in contact with Baghdad, industry sources said.

United Nations sanctions imposed on Iraq for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait place a blanket ban on export investment in the country, but the U.N. has allowed Iraq to pump $2 billion worth of oil over six months to pay for humanitarian supplies.

"Most countries are dying to get into Iraq. Most have been put off by the embargo, but countries not aligned so closely to the United States have been more aggressive," said an industry analyst who asked not to be named.
The Iraq contract was "just a beginning" as China sought to adjust its energy structure and secure supplies, said Hu Angang, a research fellow at Chinese Academy of Science.

China had debated in the early 1990s whether to import most of its crude oil, fearing huge imports could lead to heavy dependence on foreign countries. Now China has realised it can not supply its fast-growing economy domestically, Hu said.
"China's oil strategy is being adjusted. The portion of imported oil will definitely increase significantly as the economy grows," Hu, an energy specialist, said from Beijing.
The analysts said they expected Beijing to sign more oil deals with Middle East countries such as Iran to meet ballooning demand at home.
China would need to import 42 million tonnes in 2000 and 74 million tonnes in 2005, Wu estimated.
In the first four months of 1997, China imported 9.91 million tonnes of crude oil, a 44.4 percent jump from the same period a year ago, according to Chinese customs figures.
In 1996, crude oil imports rose 37.5 percent to 22 million tonnes compared with 1995 and Chinese state media have estimated that imports could reach 34 million tonnes in 1997.
"The production pace is still slow but demand is soaring. The Middle East will be the main partner for China," said Wu.
China's oil demand has been growing between six and 10 percent in recent years, compared to two percent in the United States, according to the International Energy Agency.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65 8703571)
